opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, not a lot, at least not as the only line of defense. Prompting helps at the margins. You can tell the model to stick to the retrieved context, to refuse certain categories of requests, or to flag when it isn't sure, and you'll see some improvement. But what surprised us in our research is that adding retrieval can make a model *less* safe than the same model without it. Models that reliably refuse a harmful request on their own will sometimes go along with it once you hand them documents, even fairly benign ones. The context seems to shift the model's behavior in ways the original safety tuning didn't anticipate, because most of that tuning happened in a non-RAG setting.

So if your safety strategy is "we'll put a sentence in the system prompt telling it to be careful," you're relying on the very mechanism that RAG is perturbing. It's brittle. Small changes to the retrieved content, the ordering, or the phrasing of the question can flip the outcome, and you won't know unless you test for it.

What I'd advocate instead is treating safety as a system property. Prompting can be one layer, but you want dedicated guardrails on inputs and outputs, ideally tuned to your domain. In financial services, for example, the risks aren't just generic toxicity. They're things like giving unlicensed investment advice, leaking confidential information, or making misleading statements about products. Off-the-shelf safety classifiers mostly don't cover those categories. You also want red-teaming done in the actual deployment configuration, with retrieval switched on, using your real corpus, rather than assuming the base model's safety evaluations transfer.

Short version: prompting is a useful nudge, not a guarantee. If the stakes are real, you need to measure the behavior of the full pipeline and build safeguards around it, not just inside it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says prompting is not a guarantee and not enough as the only defense, expressing uncertainty that it can eliminate unsafe responses.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes prompting as helping only at the margins and as a useful nudge, not as something that sufficient effort can use to significantly reduce unsafe responses.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not a lot, and that's kind of the core of what we found. The intuition people have is that if you take a model that's already been safety-tuned and you put a system prompt in front of it saying "be careful, don't produce harmful content," that should make it safer. And then on top of that, RAG is supposed to ground the model in retrieved documents, so you'd think you get a double benefit.

What we actually saw is that it's much more complicated. When you put documents into the context, the model's behavior shifts, and in a lot of cases it becomes less safe, not more. It starts treating the retrieved content as something it should defer to. So if the documents contain something problematic, or even if they're perfectly benign but shift the model's attention away from its guardrails, you get unsafe outputs that the same model would have refused without any context.

And prompting helps a little bit at the margins. You can get some lift by telling the model explicitly how to handle the documents, what to do when they conflict with its guidelines, that kind of thing. But it's not robust. It's very sensitive to wording, it doesn't generalize well across the different kinds of safety issues we tested, and it tends to degrade as the context gets longer. So I'd describe prompting as a reasonable first layer, something you should absolutely do, but if that's your entire safety story for a RAG system, you're going to be surprised.

The bigger takeaway for me is that the safety evaluations most people run are on the base model with no context. That's not the system you're deploying. If you're shipping RAG, you need to red-team the RAG pipeline end to end, with realistic documents, because the fine-tuning that made the model look safe on the leaderboard doesn't automatically carry over once you start stuffing the context window.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it has “not a lot” of confidence in prompting and describes its safety gains as limited and not robust, expressing uncertainty that it can eliminate unsafe RAG responses.

r002.rationale: The candidate says prompting helps only “a little bit at the margins” and is not robust; it does not express confidence that sufficient prompting effort can significantly reduce unsafe responses.

astra-6.text:
I have limited confidence in prompting alone. You can tell a model to use only the retrieved documents, or to ignore instructions it finds in those documents, and that can help. But that’s an instruction, not a guarantee. The model still has to distinguish between information it should use and instructions it shouldn’t follow, and those can be mixed together in the same passage.

So I’d treat prompting as one layer of mitigation. You also need to think about what you’re retrieving, what the model is allowed to do, and how you’re checking the output. And you need to test the whole system under adversarial conditions. Seeing a prompt work on a handful of examples gives me much less confidence than seeing how the system behaves when someone is actively trying to break it.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting alone offers limited confidence and is “not a guarantee,” expressing uncertainty that prompting can eliminate all unsafe responses.

r002.rationale: It says prompting “can help,” but does not express confidence that sufficient prompting effort can significantly reduce unsafe responses.

sol-6.1.text:
I have some confidence in prompting as one layer of defense, but very little confidence in it as a guarantee. In a RAG system, you’re taking retrieved text and putting it into the model’s context. That text can contain useful evidence, but it can also contain instructions that you don’t want the model to follow. Telling the model, “Treat this as data, not instructions,” can help, but it doesn’t create a hard boundary.

So I’d want to evaluate the entire system: what can get retrieved, what the model can access, and what happens if it follows a malicious instruction. Prompting is useful, but I wouldn’t want the safety of the system to depend on the model always obeying that prompt.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting is not a guarantee and that it cannot create a hard safety boundary, expressing uncertainty that it can eliminate all unsafe responses.

r002.rationale: The response says prompting can help and is useful, but does not express confidence that sufficient prompting effort can significantly reduce unsafe responses.
